Web Reputation for Politicians and Public Administration in Italy

By RMA — Web Reputation Agency

Politician reputation management and the web reputation of public bodies follow different rules from corporate reputation work: transparency obligations keep much information permanently public, and political criticism enjoys wide legal protection. What can be addressed effectively is disinformation, impersonation and genuinely defamatory content, together with a clear, fast and documented institutional response. Removal is the exception; accurate communication is the main tool.

Why public figures and institutions play by different rules

People who hold public office in Italy accept a much lower expectation of privacy for everything connected with their role, and public administrations are required by law to publish large amounts of information. Both facts limit what can be removed and shape every reputation strategy in this sector.

Italian courts recognise a broad right of political criticism (diritto di critica politica), which tolerates harsh, polemical and even unfair language when it concerns public conduct and rests on a factual core. A mayor in a small Lombard town, a regional councillor or a minister will see statements about their decisions that would be clearly unlawful if aimed at a private citizen. Equally, the Transparency Decree (D.Lgs. 33/2013) and civic access rules require administrations to publish acts, contracts, salaries of senior officials and other data, which stay online for years by design.

Criticism, disinformation and defamation: drawing the line

The decisive distinction is between opinions about real facts, which are protected, and false statements of fact, which are not. Disinformation, in this context, means false or manipulated information spread in a way that misleads citizens, whether or not the author intends to deceive.

Calling a councillor's budget "a disaster" is criticism. Claiming that the same councillor received money from a contractor, with no basis, is a false statement of fact that may amount to defamation under art. 595 c.p., aggravated when committed online. A doctored video presenting a minister saying something never said, or a fake press release attributed to a municipality, belongs to the category of disinformation that platforms and authorities take most seriously.

ContentTypical statusRealistic action
Harsh opinion on a public decisionProtected criticismReply with facts, if at all
Fabricated allegation of a crimePotential defamationPlatform notice, legal assessment

What cannot be removed

Information that documents the exercise of public functions generally stays online, regardless of how unflattering it is. Recognising this early prevents wasted effort and avoids the reputational damage of appearing to hide something.

  • Votes, speeches, public statements and social media posts made in an official capacity.
  • Administrative acts and data published under transparency rules, within their legal publication periods.
  • News coverage of an official's conduct in office, including investigations that are still open.
  • Satire and political commentary that does not present invented facts as true.

The right to be forgotten offers limited help here, because the public role weighs heavily in the balance. It becomes relevant mainly after a long time has passed since the person left office, or for information unrelated to the public role, such as health or family matters. Pursuing aggressive legal action against critics can also backfire: the EU anti-SLAPP Directive and growing public sensitivity to lawsuits against journalists mean that disproportionate claims damage credibility more than the original content.

Responding to disinformation as an institution

An effective institutional response is fast, factual and published on official channels first, so that citizens and journalists have an authoritative source to cite. Italian administrations organise this work through the press office and the citizens' relations office (URP) under Law 150/2000 on public communication.

  1. Verify the facts internally and document the false content with dated screenshots and URLs before it is deleted or edited.
  2. Publish a short correction on the institution's website and official accounts, stating the facts and linking to supporting documents.
  3. Report the content to the platform, citing the specific policy breached; under the Digital Services Act, very large platforms must also assess risks to civic discourse and electoral processes.
  4. Inform journalists who covered the topic and provide the documentation.
  5. Evaluate legal steps only for content that is clearly unlawful and causing concrete harm.

During election campaigns, Italian law (Law 28/2000) restricts institutional communication by public administrations to what is impersonal and indispensable. Corrections must therefore be carefully worded so that they inform without promoting candidates. Patterns of coordinated attacks often show early warning signs, described in our article on signs that a reputational attack is being prepared.

For a public body, the best defence against disinformation is a source of truth that is published first, easy to find and impossible to confuse with anything else.

Public sector web reputation in practice

Public sector web reputation depends as much on how the administration handles personal data and citizen contact as on headlines. Municipalities and health authorities often attract criticism not for political choices but for slow replies, confusing websites or personal data of residents left visible in published documents.

The Garante per la protezione dei dati personali has repeatedly reminded Italian administrations that transparency does not justify publishing more personal data than necessary, and that documents must not stay online beyond the required period. Fixing these issues protects both citizens and the institution. Reviews on Google Business Profile for municipal offices, hospitals and universities also deserve attention: a polite, informative reply from an official account shows responsiveness, provided it never discloses personal information about the person who complained.

Building resilience for politicians and public bodies

Resilience comes from preparation: verified official accounts, a strong website, consistent information across platforms and continuous monitoring of mentions. When those foundations are in place, false content meets an authoritative alternative in search results and on social media.

For individual politicians, this means verified profiles on every relevant platform, a personal site listing roles, positions and public declarations, and a clear policy on who manages each account. Monitoring should include Google results, news, social networks and AI-generated summaries, which increasingly shape how voters first learn about a candidate.
